body_markdown:
Payment gateway ROI is the net payment value a business successfully captures after accounting for transaction failures and processing costs. A lower transaction fee does not automatically deliver better ROI. If a slightly more expensive gateway completes materially more payments, the additional captured revenue can exceed the fee difference.


Here is the decision you are actually making. Provider A quotes a lower percentage. Provider B costs slightly more but completes more payment attempts. The correct comparison is net captured payment value, not the fee rate in isolation.


**Four variables drive the entire calculation:**


1. Attempted payment value
2. Payment success rate
3. Processing fee rate
4. Refund, chargeback, settlement, and recovery costs when relevant


Most pricing conversations in India stop at variable three. That is why businesses negotiate 10 basis points off a quote while losing far more value to incomplete payments. Basis points are hundredths of a percentage point, so 20 basis points means 0.20%.


This article gives you the formula, a worked example, the break-even success-rate test, a failure attribution model, and a 30-day measurement plan you can run on your own traffic.


### Key Takeaways


- Compare net captured payment value, not only the headline transaction fee.
- A small success-rate improvement can offset a larger-looking fee difference.
- New businesses can test payment gateway ROI at zero processing cost during[Razorpay’s 90-day introductory period with no platform fee](https://razorpay.com/pricing/) on domestic transactions up to Rs 5 lakh in monthly GMV, removing fee uncertainty from the evaluation entirely.
- Use attempted payment value as the denominator for a fair payment gateway ROI comparison.
- Segment success rates by payment method, issuer, ticket size, device, and time.
- Separate customer, business-integration, and gateway or bank failures before choosing a fix.
- Run a controlled test on the same traffic mix before switching providers or negotiating pricing.


## What Does Payment Gateway ROI Mean?


Payment gateway ROI measures how much payment value you successfully collect relative to the processing and operating costs required to collect it. The simplest comparison uses attempted payment value, success rate, and the fee charged on successful payments. A fuller model can also include fixed fees, settlement charges, recovery costs, refunds, and chargebacks.


Define each term before you calculate anything:


- **Attempted payment value:** Total value customers tried to pay during the selected period.
- **Successful payment value:** Value of attempts that completed successfully.
- **Processing fee:** Percentage or fixed fee charged on successful payments.
- **Net captured payment value:** Successful payment value minus payment-processing fees. It is not profit.
- **Effective cost per captured rupee:** Total payment costs divided by successful collected value.


**The basic formula:**


` text
Net captured payment value =
Attempted payment value x Success rate x (1 - Processing fee rate)`


Note what this answers and what it does not. It tells you which provider converts more of the same attempted value into money in your account. It does not tell you your margin, because product cost, fulfilment, tax, and operating expenses sit outside it. A lower merchant discount rate, the commission deducted on a successful payment, improves this number only when success rates hold steady. For the underlying metric mechanics, see the Razorpay guide to[payment success rate](https://razorpay.com/blog/payment-success-rate-tips-to-improve) .


## When Does a Higher Success Rate Beat a Lower Transaction Fee?


A higher success rate beats a lower transaction fee when the additional payment value successfully collected is greater than the extra processing cost. The break-even uplift can be much smaller than most businesses expect, often a fraction of a single percentage point.


### Illustrative Scenario, Not a Provider Quote or Market Benchmark


Assumptions used below are hypothetical arithmetic inputs:


- Rs 1 crore in attempted payment value per month
- Provider A charges 1.8% and records an 88% success rate
- Provider B charges 2.0% and records a 91% success rate
- GST, refunds, chargebacks, settlement charges, and operating costs are excluded to isolate the fee-versus-success-rate relationship
- Processing fees apply only to successful payment value


Metric Provider A: Lower Fee Provider B: Higher Success


Attempted payment value Rs 1,00,00,000 Rs 1,00,00,000


Illustrative success rate 88% 91%


Successful payment value Rs 88,00,000 Rs 91,00,000


Illustrative processing rate 1.8% 2.0%


Processing fee Rs 1,58,400 Rs 1,82,000


Net captured payment value Rs 86,41,600 Rs 89,18,000


Net advantage Baseline Rs 2,76,400 more


Read the result carefully. Provider B charges Rs 23,600 more in processing fees. It still captures Rs 2,76,400 more after processing fees because more payment attempts succeed. Note also that 88% to 91% is a 3 percentage-point increase, not a 3% increase.


This example does not prove that every higher-priced provider performs better. It shows how to test whether the uplift is financially sufficient on your own numbers, over a period and payment mix that genuinely represent your business.


### The Break-Even Success-Rate Formula


` text
Required success rate for Provider B =
Provider A success rate x (1 - Provider A fee rate) / (1 - Provider B fee rate)`


Using the illustrative assumptions, Provider B needs a success rate above approximately 88.18% to offset a 2.0% fee versus Provider A at 1.8% and 88% success. An uplift of roughly 0.18 percentage points reaches break-even before other costs.


That is the number worth remembering. The fee gap looks like 0.2 percentage points of cost. The performance gap needed to neutralise it is smaller than most teams assume, which is exactly why fee-only negotiation is an incomplete strategy.


### What Changes When GST Is Included?


In India, 18% GST applies to the processing fee, not the payment value. Adding it makes a 1.8% fee cost 2.124% effectively, and a 2.0% fee cost 2.36%. Rerunning the illustrative break-even with GST on the fee moves the required rate from about 88.18% to about 88.21%, an uplift requirement of roughly 0.21 percentage points. Verify current tax treatment against the live[Razorpay pricing](https://razorpay.com/pricing/) page before relying on these figures.


### Did You Know?


On Rs 1 crore in attempted payment value, each one percentage point of additional success represents Rs 1 lakh in gross captured payment value before processing fees. This is arithmetic, not an industry benchmark.


**PRO-TIP:** Run this calculation with your own payment mix. A blended result can hide a strong UPI route and a weak card route, or the reverse.

## Which Payment Metrics Must You Keep Separate?


Five metrics are used interchangeably and should not be. Each has a different denominator, and swapping one for another produces a false ROI comparison.


Metric Numerator Denominator What It Tells You


Payment success rate Successful payment attempts Total valid payment attempts Infrastructure and payment completion performance


Authorisation rate Approved authorisation requests Total authorisation requests Issuer and risk-decision performance


Checkout conversion rate Completed payments Customers who entered checkout End-to-end customer journey performance


Recovery rate Failed payments later recovered Eligible failed payments targeted Effectiveness of retry or recovery activity


Uptime Available service time Total measured service time Availability, not transaction completion


A high uptime percentage does not guarantee a high payment success rate. A service can be fully available while an issuer, network, or route degrades and declines eligible payments.


Checkout conversion includes user behaviour that happens before a payment attempt even exists, which is why it is not a gateway performance measure. Do not compare two providers unless both use the same event definitions and the same exclusions. For the taxonomy behind failure data, see the Razorpay[payment error source fields](https://razorpay.com/docs/errors/payments/list/) .


## Where Does Payment ROI Leak? Diagnose Failures Before Changing Providers


Payment ROI leaks at four points: customer-side declines, your own integration errors, gateway or bank failures, and abandoned checkouts that never created a payment attempt. Only some of those are a provider problem, so attribute each failure to its source before you assume a switch will recover the revenue.


### Attribute Each Failure Before Assigning Blame


Failure Source Typical Signal Correct Owner ROI Action


Customer Wrong OTP, cancellation, insufficient funds Customer experience and product teams Clear messages, alternate method, safe retry


Business Invalid request, missing field, wrong amount, disabled method Engineering and payments teams Fix integration before judging provider performance


Gateway or bank Transient processing or bank-side error Payments infrastructure team Retry, fallback, alternate route, downtime monitoring


Internal or platform Processing error returned by the platform itself Payments infrastructure team Retry after a short delay, monitor frequency


Razorpay error responses include a source field that distinguishes these origins and indicates who should act. Method-level reports can carry additional values for issuer, network, or beneficiary bank conditions, so read the field rather than assuming a single cause.


### Separate Payment Failure From Checkout Abandonment


Checkout abandonment means the customer never created a valid payment attempt. It affects conversion but should not be counted as a gateway transaction failure. Documented cart abandonment averages[70.22% across 50 studies](https://baymard.com/lists/cart-abandonment-rate) , and much of it reflects browsing, price comparison, and saving items for later rather than payment breakage.


### Separate First-Attempt Success From Recovery


An unrecovered failure is a first attempt that fails where the customer never retries successfully. Recovery tooling can create real value even when first-attempt success rates do not change. Report the two separately, or recovery activity will be misread as improved gateway performance.


A provider change cannot fix a malformed payment request, an unclear checkout message, or every customer-side decline. Diagnose the source before attributing all lost revenue to the gateway.


> **PRO-TIP:** Build a weekly failure waterfall showing customer, business, and gateway or bank errors. Assign one owner and one next action to each category.


## How Should You Segment Payment Success Rates?


Segment before you compare. A single blended success rate is the easiest way to reach the wrong provider decision, because it averages away the routes that are actually costing you money.


Work through this checklist:


1. Payment method and subtype
2. Issuer or bank
3. Acquirer or route, where available
4. Ticket-size band
5. Device, operating system, and app or web flow
6. Geography
7. Hour of day and day of week
8. New versus returning customer
9. First attempt versus retry
10. Soft decline versus hard decline


### Why Weighted Averages Can Mislead


A provider may show a better overall rate only because it processes more of its volume on the easiest payment method. That is a mix effect, not a performance advantage. The fair comparison uses the same transaction mix or a normalised model that reweights each provider to your actual distribution of attempted value.


Ticket-size banding deserves particular attention, because low-ticket, mid-ticket, and high-ticket payments often behave differently on both cost and completion.


### Did You Know?


A one-point improvement on a payment method that represents 60% of attempted value has six times the gross revenue impact of the same improvement on a method representing 10%. This is arithmetic based on mix, not an external performance claim.


## How to Run a Fair 30-Day Payment Gateway ROI Test


Follow this procedure in order:


1. **Define the denominator.** Use valid payment attempts and attempted payment value. Document exclusions before the test starts.
2. **Establish a baseline.** Export at least 30 days of success rate, attempted value, captured value, fees, refunds, and chargebacks by payment method.
3. **Normalise the traffic mix.** Compare the same payment methods, ticket-size bands, devices, issuers, and time periods.
4. **Split or phase traffic safely.** Use percentage routing or a controlled migration so campaign, seasonality, and traffic-quality differences do not distort the result.
5. **Track first attempts and recovered attempts separately.** This prevents recovery activity from being mistaken for first-attempt gateway performance.
6. **Calculate net captured payment value.** Apply the same cost inclusions to each provider.
7. **Review failure-source distribution.** Confirm whether observed gains came from routing, integration fixes, checkout changes, or customer retries.
8. **Set a decision threshold before the test.** Define the minimum net captured revenue uplift required to justify integration, contract, and operational change.


### What This Test Cannot Prove


An uncontrolled before-and-after comparison cannot establish provider causation. Do not compare a sale week with a normal week, or one provider’s UPI-heavy traffic with another provider’s card-heavy traffic. If the mix and the period are not matched, the difference you measure may simply be your own traffic, not the gateway.


## Payment Gateway ROI Scorecard: What Should You Compare?


Decision Factor Measurement Weight Guidance


Net captured payment value Successful value minus processing fees Highest


Success rate by payment method Successful attempts divided by valid attempts High


Effective cost per captured rupee Total payment costs divided by collected value High


Recovery performance Eligible failed payments later completed Medium


Integration and maintenance effort Engineering hours and incident workload Medium


Settlement and working-capital impact Time and cost to access funds Medium


Refund and chargeback cost Fees, reversals, holds, and operational effort Medium


Reporting and reconciliation quality Time required to close and explain payments Supporting


Set your own weights. An ecommerce brand may prioritise checkout conversion and failure recovery, while a B2B platform may prioritise high-ticket reliability, reconciliation, and settlement predictability.


Also model promotional pricing as a time-bound input. Rerun the break-even calculation at the post-promotion rate, and review the full cost checklist in this explainer on[transparent payment gateway pricing](https://razorpay.com/blog/payment-gateway-transparent-pricing-explained/) .


## What This Model Excludes


Net captured payment value is not profit. The simplified model leaves out product and fulfilment cost, taxes beyond fee-level GST, refunds, chargebacks, customer acquisition cost, and migration and engineering effort. It also treats attempted payment value loosely, because repeated attempts by the same customer can inflate the denominator and overstate recoverable revenue.


## The Decision Rule: Choose the Highest Net Captured Value, Not the Lowest Quote


Three steps close the decision:


1. Calculate each provider’s net captured payment value on the same traffic mix.
2. Confirm that the improvement persists by payment method and over a representative period.
3. Subtract migration, integration, settlement, refund, chargeback, and operating costs before making the final call.


A lower fee is valuable only when payment performance is comparable. If a higher-success payment platform captures more net value after all costs, it delivers the stronger ROI.


Review your last 30 days of payment attempts, calculate the break-even success-rate uplift, and evaluate routing or platform changes against net captured payment value.


## Frequently Asked Questions


### **1. How do I calculate payment gateway ROI?**


Use net captured payment value: attempted payment value multiplied by payment success rate, then reduced by the applicable processing fee. For a fuller comparison, add fixed fees, recovery costs, refunds, chargebacks, settlement charges, and operating effort consistently for each provider.


### **2. How much success-rate improvement offsets a 0.2% higher transaction fee?**


It depends on the current success rate. At an illustrative 88% success rate, moving from a 1.8% fee to a 2.0% fee requires roughly 88.18% success to break even before other costs. Use the formula above with your actual figures.


### **3. Is payment success rate the same as checkout conversion rate?**


No. Payment success rate measures completed payments against valid payment attempts. Checkout conversion measures completed payments against customers who entered checkout, including customers who left before creating a payment attempt.


### **4. Should I choose the payment gateway with the lowest transaction fee?**


Only when success rates, fixed fees, settlement costs, recovery, and operational effort are comparable. A lower rate can produce weaker ROI if more customers fail to complete payment or if the payment platform adds other material costs.


### **5. How can smart routing improve payment gateway ROI?**


Smart routing can direct eligible transactions through routes selected for success, cost, or a blended objective. Retry and fallback logic may give failed payments another valid path transiently, while percentage routing can support controlled testing and cost management.
